title: Krishna Grants Shishupala's Mother the Boon of a Hundred Offences
story:
To understand the king who now stood raging in the hall at Indraprastha, Bhishma said, one had to go back to his birth, in the city of Chedi.

The child born to the king of Chedi had three eyes and four hands. The moment he drew breath, he screamed and brayed like an ass, and the sound of it struck fear into his father, his mother, and all their kin. Such omens were not to be borne; his parents resolved to abandon him.

Then an incorporeal voice spoke to the king and his wife, with their ministers and priests, all with hearts paralyzed by anxiety. "This son of yours, O king," the voice said, "will become both fortunate and superior in strength. Therefore you have no fear from him. Cherish the child without anxiety. He will not die in childhood; his time is not yet come. He that will slay him with weapons has also been born."

The mother, rendered anxious by affection for her son, bowed and asked the invisible being: "I desire to hear who will be the slayer of this my son." And the voice answered: "He upon whose lap this child, being placed, his superfluous arms fall down upon the ground like a pair of five-headed snakes, and at the sight of whom the third eye on his forehead disappears — he will be his slayer."

Hearing of the child with three eyes and four arms, and of the words of the invisible being, all the kings of the earth went to Chedi to behold him. The king of Chedi, worshipping the monarchs as each deserved, placed his child upon their laps one after another. And though the child passed through the laps of a thousand kings, the sign that the voice had promised did not come to pass.

Word of the wonder reached Dwaravati, and the mighty Yadava heroes, Balarama and Krishna, set out to see their father's sister, that daughter of the Yadavas who was queen of Chedi. They saluted everyone according to his rank, and the king and queen, and asked after everyone's welfare; and when the heroes had been worshipped, the queen, with great pleasure, herself placed the child on the lap of Krishna.

As soon as the child was placed on his lap, the superfluous arms fell to the ground, and the eye on his forehead disappeared. And the queen, beholding it, was filled with alarm and anxiety, and begged Krishna for a boon. "O mighty-armed Krishna," she said, "I am afflicted with fear. Grant me a boon. You are the assurer of all afflicted ones, the dispeller of everyone's fear."

Krishna said: "Fear not, O respected one. You are acquainted with morality; you need have no fear from me. What boon shall I give you? What shall I do, O aunt? Whether able or not, I shall do your bidding."

The queen said: "You will have to pardon the offences of Shishupala for my sake. O tiger of the Yadu race, know that even this is the boon I ask."

And Krishna said: "O aunt, even when he will deserve to be slain, I will pardon a hundred offences of his. Grieve not."

So the old story ran, told that day in the hall at Indraprastha while the king of Chedi stood before the assembly, burning with pride in that very promise. "Even thus, O Bhima," Bhishma said, turning to the sons of Pandu, "is this wretch of a king, Shishupala of wicked heart, who, proud of the boon granted by Govinda, summons you to battle."

The hundred offences had been counted out over the years, in slights and mockeries and open insults. And the count, Bhishma did not need to say, was nearly spent.
reflection: A mother's plea converts an omen of death into a hundred pardons, and the child's own body marks his slayer the moment Krishna touches him. The boon does not erase the sign; it only postpones it — and the hundred offences, counted out over a lifetime, are what make the final reckoning possible.
next_story_tease: The hundred pardons were nearly spent — and the sacrifice that had gathered them all to Indraprastha had first been announced, long before, in Dwaraka.
hero_scene: In the palace of Chedi, the queen sets the three-eyed, four-armed child upon Krishna's lap — the child's superfluous arms falling away like snakes and the third eye fading, as the mother watches in alarm and hope.
